Introduction

Beneath every glossy exterior beats a heart riddled with holes.

— a must-use line for any lyrical essay in China’s college entrance exam

Cars are no exception.

To achieve good sound insulation, many carmakers apply damping material to reduce body vibration and, with it, the noise the body radiates.

The goal

Acoustically optimize a car body that already had damping patches.

Meet the acoustic requirements with the lowest weight, the lowest cost and the least damping material.

The requirements

  • Quickly identify undamped panels and areas

  • Check that the existing damping patches are the right size and thickness

  • Remove unnecessary patches

  • Demonstrate the result

A colleague of mine was told to reach the goal and meet all the requirements within a week, whatever it takes. So he ran tests by day and processed data in his hotel by night, and, incredibly, got it done within the week.

So the question is: how did he do it?

There are roughly three existing approaches:

1. Accelerometers, strain gauges or microphones

  • Low resolution

  • Time-consuming

2. Scanning laser vibrometer

  • Expensive

  • Hard to use efficiently

3. Acoustic scanning

  • Quick and convenient

  • High resolution

  • Accurate: at the surface of a vibrating object, the surface velocity and the acoustic particle velocity are linearly related

So our man made a snap decision: scan, and measure the velocity!

If you are not familiar with particle velocity, or with measuring it using Microflown sensors, see this earlier article on our WeChat account:

Particle velocity: there is more to sound than sound pressure

But why should the particle velocity in the air have anything to do with the vibration velocity of a surface? And what exactly is the relationship?

We checked, and yes, there is one.

On the axis of a circular piston, the measured particle velocity u_n and the surface velocity v_n are related as follows [1]:

It has been shown [2] that when the distance δ between the measurement point and the vibrating surface is very small, the last two factors in the expression for u_n have very little effect. In other words, u_n and v_n are then nearly equal. So as long as we measure very close to the surface, the particle velocity can stand in for the vibration velocity of the surface.

That means wherever the particle velocity near an area is high, that area needs a patch.

The Scan & Paint 2D scanning system

In practice, he used Microflown’s Scan & Paint 2D system [3]. A sound intensity probe (one microphone plus one Microflown particle velocity sensor) is swept over the surface while a camera records its position, and the system produces an image directly. I described the scanning technique in detail in this article:

Scan & Paint: 2D and 3D scanning that lets you see sound

The experiment

To rule out interference, the powertrain was removed for the tests. The excitation came from an omnidirectional sound source.

The main measurement areas were:

Without any damping material, the scans clearly reveal the modes of the car floor in several low-frequency bands. The darker areas are therefore where the patches need to do their work.

In the figure below, the areas outlined with white dashed lines are where the original patches sat. But the patches weren’t all put where they count: some were unnecessary, and some were downright ineffective.

The next figure makes it even clearer.

Across: baseline, with the original patches; undamped, with all the original patches removed; optimised, after optimization, with only one patch left (white boxes mark the remaining patch, white crosses the patches removed).

Down: with carpet; without carpet (take a guess ;)).

As you can see, once the carpet is in, there is no difference between baseline and undamped. A real car always has a carpet, so that whole pile of patches was doing nothing. Only one area in the lower middle shows noticeable noise, so a single patch there is all you need.

Road test

The re-patched Bentley hits the road!

The tests were run on two road surfaces of different roughness.

Across almost the entire frequency range, the interior sound pressure level of the optimized Bentley did not go up; it actually went down. In other words, optimizing the layout of the damping material really did improve the sound insulation.

At the same time, the number of patches went down by 15%, which cut the cost by 15% and the total weight by about 10% [4].

Take them away, no need to thank us!

Conclusion

Bentley is happy.

By near-field scanning with a Microflown sound intensity probe to measure particle velocity, and so map the vibration of the body surface, we finished the homework set by Papa Bentley (in Chinese engineering slang, the client is always “papa”) within five days. Weight and cost went down, and the sound insulation requirement was not just met but exceeded.

References

  1. ^Beissner, K. “On the plane‐wave approximation of acoustic intensity.” The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 71, no. 6 (1982): 1406–1411

  2. ^de Bree, H. E. “The very near field theory, simulations and measurements of sound pressure and particle velocity in the very near field.” In 11th International Congress on Sound and Vibration, 2004.

  3. ^https://www.microflown.com/products/sound-localization-systems/scan-paint-2d/

  4. ^Fernandez Comesana, D, Tatlow, J. Designing the damping treatment of a vehicle body based on scanning particle velocity measurements [C]. Aachen Acoustics Colloquium, 2019.
